title: PSS 3.1 Opens New Possibilities for Hardware and Software Verification
gist: Accellera approved the Portable Test and Stimulus Standard (PSS) 3.1 on November 11, its first update since PSS 3.0 in August 2024, adding generic/soft constraints, action overriding, software-integration features, standardized heterogeneous execution (typed FIFO channels, target execution units), and richer address/register modeling to make verification intent reusable across simulation, emulation, FPGA prototyping and post-silicon.

insights.claim: Accellera approved the Portable Test and Stimulus Standard (PSS) 3.1, announced November 11, the first update since PSS 3.0 in August 2024.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Standards updates set the feature baseline EDA vendors' portable-stimulus tools must support.
insights.locator: Accellera’s approval of the Portable Test and Stimulus Standard

insights.claim: PSS lets engineers describe verification intent in a high-level, implementation-independent model and realize it across simulation, emulation, FPGA prototyping and post-silicon validation, reducing rebuilt work across project stages.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Reusable verification content lowers verification cost, the dominant share of chip development effort.

insights.claim: PSS 3.1 adds generic constraints (replacing deprecated dynamic constraints), soft constraints that set overridable defaults, enhanced array-slice operations, and inline initialization of non-randomized action attributes.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Teams with large scenario libraries gain maintainability; migration work needed where dynamic constraints are used.
insights.locator: One of the release’s most promising advances

insights.claim: PSS 3.1 introduces action overriding in component subtypes, mutable component attributes, instance-qualified component references and multi-dimensional arrays of component instances, easing modeling of regular structures like CPU clusters or multi-channel DMA engines.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Improves reuse across product families, relevant to SoC vendors with many derivative chips.
insights.quote: With action overriding, an activity can be written against a base action, much like an interface.
insights.locator: Reuse also benefits from new customization mechanisms.

insights.claim: PSS 3.1 adds exported functions for target callbacks, exec block tags to remove duplicate generated code, a general annotation mechanism, mustache-style string templates, and a standard message() function with verbosity levels that logs identically during solving and on-target execution.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Eliminating tool-specific print mechanisms reduces vendor lock-in for verification teams.
insights.quote: so teams no longer need a tool-specific print mechanism for each target
insights.locator: The release also recognizes software’s expanding role

insights.claim: PSS 3.1 standardizes heterogeneous execution: typed FIFO channels let concurrent test code on different executors exchange data, and target execution units assign each executor's generated code to a named output file in C, C++ or SystemVerilog.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Moves multi-core test setup from vendor-specific to standard, enabling target-environment reuse across tools.
insights.quote: Because this setup is now defined by the standard rather than by each vendor, the same target environment can be reused across tools.
insights.locator: Support for heterogeneous execution is another welcome development.

insights.claim: For an SoC pairing a RISC-V core with a DSP, PSS 3.1 lets each core's test code go into its own source file built with different compilers while SystemVerilog transactor actions sit together in testbench code.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous RISC-V-plus-accelerator SoCs are a growing verification burden that the standard now addresses.
insights.locator: In an SoC that pairs a RISC-V core with a DSP

insights.claim: PSS 3.1 expands address and register modeling with shared address claims, negative address offsets (mapping one physical space to different virtual addresses per CPU), extensible memory-access controls, register collections and symbolic register names tied to the project's software stack.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Better fit for complex SoC memory maps reduces hand-maintained hard-coded addresses.

insights.claim: Upgrading to PSS 3.1 breaks some existing models: access functions such as write32 take an extra memory-access descriptor argument, annotation/overlap/mutable/soft become reserved keywords, and dynamic constraints are deprecated.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Expect migration effort and staggered tool adoption before PSS 3.1 features are broadly usable.
insights.locator: Teams upgrading existing models should note

insights.claim: Accellera supports PSS adoption with a 16-part Learning PSS video series plus tutorials, workshops, examples and the Portable Stimulus Community Forum.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Ecosystem investment indicates continued push to broaden portable-stimulus adoption.
